article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Fresh off directing The Beekeeper 2 for Miramax , Timo Tjahjanto has come aboard to direct The Burnout for the studio, sources tell Deadline.

Interesting comps here: The Burnout is billed as The Big Lebowski meets Jason Bourne . In the film, a washed-up former CIA agent, now living as a carefree burnout in Ibiza, is reluctantly dragged back into action.

With its “back-in-action” framing, the film also feels in the vein of the Nobody actioners starring Bob Odenkirk, the second of which was directed by Tjahjanto.

Sources said the script — by Tom O’Connor, with current revisions by Hunter Toro — was brought into Miramax by Arianna D’Andrea, VP Film Production & Development. The project falls in line with Miramax CEO Jonathan Glickman’s mission to develop originals for film and TV while finding the right opportunities to mine the studio’s expansive IP library.

Watch on Deadline

A genre filmmaker from Indonesia, Tjahjanto first garnered attention when he teamed with Gareth Evans to direct segment “Safe Haven” for V/H/S/2 . He followed that up with The Night Comes for Us — an homage to 1980s Hong Kong action cinema, which became Netflix’s first Indonesian original — plus horror film May the Devil Take You , premiering both of those titles at Fantastic Fest.

In the last few years, Tjahjanto has risen to become an in-demand studio filmmaker, with work on Nobody 2 and The Beekeeper 2 , the sequel to the acclaimed Jason Statham action thriller that grossed over $162M worldwide. The new installment is slated for release by Amazon MGM Studios on January 15, 2027. Currently in production on an untitled Indonesian thriller for Netflix, Tjahjanto is represented by WME, Entertainment 360 and attorney Marios Rush.

Over the summer, Miramax released its first Scary Movie in 13 years, with the Paramount horror spoof posting the biggest R-rated comedy opening in almost the entire span of the franchise’s absence — going on to more than $230 million worldwide. In television, the studio is fresh off the release of Guy Ritchie’s The Gentlemen Season 2, which debuted to 6.7 million global views, elevating from No. 3 on the global English-language TV chart to No. 1 in its second week.

Other upcoming film projects for Miramax include the Will Smith action thriller Supermax , a Serendipity redo, and Frankie Shaw’s 4 Kids Walk Into a Bank , all for Amazon MGM. Additionally, there’s an adaptation of the Amy Taylor novel Ruins , starring Vanessa Kirby and Sebastian Stan, the Statham-led action thriller John Doe , and James DeMonaco’s thriller Vigilant .

SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “ You Can See Everything ,” now playing in theaters.

“You Can See Everything” may rewrite the rules of the Oscar season.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s A24 documentary, which follows the Theranos founder through the 34 days before she reported to prison and keeps rolling afterward, opened to a staggering $15 million over the weekend , a number most nonfiction films never see in a full run. It’s also boasting a record-setting 99 on Metacritic, 98% on Rotten Tomatoes and holding a 4.7 (out of 5) on Letterboxd and 9.4 on IMDb (as of Monday, Oct. 19). If the IMDb score holds, it will surpass the longstanding No. 1 “The Shawshank Redemption” (1994) as the highest-rated film of all time.

In addition to being eligible for best documentary feature at the 99th Academy Awards, the film will also be submitted across the board as seen on A24’s awards site: best picture (Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, Tatiana Bears, Maggie Ambrose and Jack Davis), director (Fielder and Oppenheim), production design (Alex DiGerlando and Rebecca Meis), cinematography (David Bolen), costume design (Katina Danabassis), film editing (Adam Locke-Norton), makeup and hairstyling (Stephanie Pasicov and Kerrie Smith), sound (Paul Hsu and Richard Carlos) and original score (Ari Balouzian).

Variety confirmed exclusively after the film made its surprise world premiere (and general existence became known) at the Telluride Film Festival that Amanda Seyfried , credited in the film as Elizabeth Holmes, is eligible for the Academy Awards in the acting categories. Seyfried, who also appears as herself while reprising her Emmy-winning turn as Holmes from “The Dropout,” will be campaigned in the supporting actress category. If she lands the nomination, it would be her second, following “Mank” (2020). She would get there for playing two people at once: herself and the woman she already won an Emmy statue for playing.

Fielder, credited as himself, may be eligible to submit as a performer, but Variety has confirmed he won’t. The decision sidesteps a bit of history that has never gone a performer’s way: no actor has been nominated for an Oscar for playing himself. The closest the Academy came recently was with another A24 title, “Sing Sing” (2024), in which co-writer and star Clarence Maclin, a formerly incarcerated man playing a version of himself, built a real case for supporting actor and was ultimately overlooked. Fielder’s possible Oscar recognition would be in three categories — best picture, documentary feature and directing.

Christopher Abbott, who also appears in the film as Holmes’ spouse, Billy Evans, in recreated scenes, is also eligible for acting consideration in the supporting actor category.

Sources close to the awards campaign say the acting push will center on Seyfried regardless.

No documentary has ever been nominated for best picture in 98 ceremonies. The zeitgeist says this one can be. The awards circuit that usually paves the way is another matter.

We are in uncharted waters.

Variety Awards Circuit: Oscars

Golden Globes : Not eligible based on current written rules, but there could be an avenue.

The Globes don’t recognize documentaries, which means no picture, no director and no Seyfried. The film cannot be submitted in any category. However, with the acting eligibilities lingering, sources share the group may consider it for this upcoming run. That doesn’t mean it can be eligible across the board. And then in that case, do they consider it a drama or comedy/musical?

Critics Choice Awards : Eligible across the board, including the acting races.

That makes Critics Choice the only major stop this season where the performances in “You Can See Everything” could get significant recognition before Oscar nominations.

Actor Awards : Not eligible but could they make an exception?

The ceremony formerly known as the SAG Awards does not recognize documentaries, since they aren’t narrative films, even with the narrative recreations woven throughout this one. Seyfried’s path to a supporting actress nomination looked like it would skip the precursor vote by her fellow actors. However, the committee that rules on films is said to be looking at the film to see if it can, in fact, be eligible.

BAFTA : Still a bit of a question mark but it doesn’t look promising.

The current rules and guidelines indicate the film can submit in the top categories, but sources say BAFTA may not go for it. Whether Seyfried and Fielder can enter the acting races is less clear. However, indications suggest it may ultimately be eligible for recognition if the voters choose to go for it.

Writers Guild of America : Not eligible.

The film has no credited screenplay, which isn’t unusual for a documentary but isn’t universal either. Michael Moore’s “Bowling for Columbine” famously won the WGA’s original screenplay prize more than 20 years ago. That won’t be the case here, so “You Can See Everything” won’t be eligible for the Oscars ‘ original or adapted screenplay categories.

Directors Guild of America : Eligible in both top categories.

This is where it gets interesting. The DGA has a separate documentary category, and its top prize is labeled for directors of a theatrically released feature film. Questions began percolating because of RaMell Ross, whose “Hale County This Morning, This Evening” was nominated for documentary feature at the Oscars before his narrative debut, “Nickel Boys,” was entered in first-time feature director at the DGA, a category he went on to win.

This is Fielder’s first directorial credit for a documentary feature, but that isn’t the case for Oppenheim, who helmed “Spermworld” (2024) and “Some Kind of Heaven” (2020). Therefore, the film won’t be eligible for first-time feature director. However, Oppenheim makes his narrative feature directorial debut with the A24 thriller “Primetime” starring Robert Pattinson, Merritt Wever and Skyler Gisondo. He will be vying for one of the five slots in that category.

More importantly, under the forward-facing rules, Fielder and Oppenheim are eligible for the DGA’s top award in addition to the documentary prize. That means they could take a slot otherwise slotted for Christopher Nolan (“The Odyssey”) or the other directing duos in the race, including Los Javis (“La Bola Negra”) and Phil Lord and Chris Miller (“Project Hail Mary”).

ACE Eddies : Eligible

The guild that represents film editing separates theatrical feature films into four categories: drama, comedy, documentary and animated. Per the rules, “You Can See Everything” would have to choose a category to submit to. A similar situation occurred with Jonas Poher Rasmussen’s animated nonfiction film “Flee” (2021), which was submitted to the guild as a documentary and nominated by ACE Eddie.

ASC (American Society of Cinematographers) : Eligible, but only as a documentary.

Per the rules for the highest award for cinematographers, “All Documentary Feature Films and Documentary Series Episodes must be submitted in the Documentary Award category.”

Producers Guild of America : Eligible for both the theatrical motion picture award and the documentary prize.

Add it up and you get a contender with no conventional map. Best picture winners typically announce themselves through the guilds, with a PGA win, a DGA nod, an Actor Awards ensemble slot and a Globe or two along the way. “You Can See Everything” likely won’t be at the Globes. The actors can’t nominate it. BAFTA would be a stop if the rules hold. That leaves the DGA, PGA and Critics Choice as the only places the film can win a top prize and signal whether it’s a historic nominee or something bigger.

And this raises a bigger question: What if the first documentary nominated for best picture goes all the way to the top prize?

A few studios are trying to frame the race as David vs. Goliath regarding how they can possibly topple Christopher Nolan’s billion-dollar sensation “The Odyssey.” What if this is actually Odysseus vs. Elizabeth Holmes?

A caveat that applies to all of the above: every voting body and guild writes its own rules, and any of them can convene a committee to revisit eligibility. So all of these are subject to change.

Holmes built a company on the promise that one test could see everything . Awards season has at least six major contests, and as of now, none of them can agree on what they’re actually looking at.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Vertical has acquired North American rights to horror film Recluse , the Tribeca title executive-produced by Spooky Pictures’ Steven Schneider ( Paranormal Activity ).

The feature debut of writer-director Henry Chaisson ( Servant ), stars Sasha Frolova, Xander Berkeley, Toby Poser, Mia Vallet, Kimball Farley, and Frankie Seratch. Vertical will release the film theatrically in the first half of 2027.

The synopsis for the well-reviewed title reads: “After a fire leaves her estranged father injured, Joan (Frolova) begins hearing mysterious audio recordings related to her mother’s disappearance years earlier. Returning home, she works to piece together the mystery of her mother’s final days. Joan realizes that her mother’s vanishing meshes with a larger tapestry of tragedy that has plagued their family over the years. And the closer she gets to unearthing the truth, the more somebody else fights to keep it buried.”

Related Stories

Vertical Wraps Up Domestic On Alex Moffat & Julia Stiles Comedy 'Unbearable Christmas'

Vertical Saves Lily James & Pierce Brosnan Starring 'Cliffhanger'; Spring 2027 U.S. Release Eyed - TIFF

Pic is a co-production between Points North and Restricted Pictures, which are currently in post on the genre project Night After Night . The film was produced by Josh Lobo, Gillian Cooper, Alex Dandino, Henry Chaisson, and Katharina Windemuth and executive-produced by Cailla O’Shea, Frankie Seratch, Sasha Frolova, and Steven Schneider.

Watch on Deadline

The deal was negotiated by SVP of Acquisitions Tony Piantedosi and Manager of Acquisitions Rachel White on behalf of Vertical and by Mike Chapman from Blue Finch Films on behalf of the filmmakers.

“Making Recluse was an extraordinary journey alongside a truly exceptional cast and crew, and seeing it connect with audiences at Tribeca, Fantasia and FrightFest has been hugely rewarding,” stated Chaisson. “I’m thrilled to be partnering with Vertical to bring it to the big screen.”

“ Recluse gets under your skin, then claws its way back out. Oh, and it leaves a scar,” added Schneider. “Henry Chaisson delivers the goods for Vertical, which has quietly become a new home for high-quality horror.”

“Henry, along with legendary horror producer Steven Schneider, has crafted a chilling, atmospheric thriller that will keep audiences on edge,” said Vertical Partner Peter Jarowey. “After strong festival showings including its world premiere at Tribeca, we’re thrilled to bring Recluse to theaters next year.”

Additional below-the-line talent includes cinematographer Bryce Holden, editors Chaisson and Nik Voytas, costume designer Katharina Windemuth, and production designer Yulanda Yo-Rong Shieh, with music by Chaisson.

Feature

Why Do Horror Films Have Such a Hold on Our Imaginations?

An exhibition at the Academy Museum explores the transgressive power of scary movies, channeling our deepest fears about life, death, and the unknown.

The Horror Show at the Academy Museum (all photos Matt Stromberg/

Hyperallergic unless noted)

LOS ANGELES — Horror films may have historically been relegated to second-class status in the cinematic canon, viewed by some critics as vulgar fright fests that lack the gravitas of “serious” filmmaking. But there is no denying the captivating power they have exerted over audiences, channeling our deepest fears about life, death, the world around us, and the unknown onto the silver screen. Now on view through July at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures in Los Angeles, The Horror Show takes a broad look at the history of the genre, exploring why scary movies have had such a hold on our imaginations — and prompting a reconsideration of their place in the filmic pantheon.

It all began with a single object: Dracula’s cape. That is, the original iconic cape worn by Bela Lugosi in Todd Browning’s Dracula (1931), which the Academy acquired from the Lugosi family in 2019. “It’s been a family heirloom for several generations,” Jessica Niebel, senior curator at the museum, told Hyperallergic . “We knew we wanted to highlight it in a special way.”

Dracula (1931) © Academy Museum Foundation, photo Emily Shur)

Once they had this cornerstone of the exhibition, curators began to assemble a wide range of material, including costumes, props, concept art, film posters, and scripts, from horror classics ( The Shining, Psycho ), contemporary masterpieces ( Midsommar , Get Out ) and underrated gems ( Tales From the Hood , The Stuff ). Centering both visual and narrative artistry, the curators drew heavily on the Academy Museum’s own robust collection, as well as objects and archival materials borrowed from dozens of lenders.

article_text:
Films and events

Official Competition

The Idiot(s)

Aimee Lou Wood and Johnny Flynn are superb as Anna and Fyodor Dostoevsky in Małgorzata Szumowska and Michał Englert’s acerbic and joyful period film.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Directors Małgorzata Szumowska, Michał Englert

Screenwriters Małgorzata Szumowska, Michał Englert, Kasper Bajon, Brid Arnstein

With Aimee Lou Wood, Johnny Flynn, Vicky Krieps

Germany-Poland 2026. 118min

Courtesy of The Match Factory

Languages English, French, German With English subtitles

Introduction

Anna Dostoevsky loves her husband Fyodor. Fyodor loves his wife, but he also loves gambling and booze. Living in self-imposed exile in Germany, Fyodor’s biggest obstacle to creative progress is himself. Anna tries desperately to rid him of his procrastination so he can deliver a new novel and they can avoid destitution. Sending up the myth of the male genius, The Idiot(s) is also a beautiful love story about the writer and the wife that saved him.

Grace Barber-Plentie

Content advice

Contains scenes of infant death, nudity, and sex.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

La Dérive

The debut of French New Wave filmmaker Paula Delsol fell into oblivion, but her essential contribution to cinema is now ready for rediscovery.

Possible Love

Lee Chang-dong’s masterfully directed follow-up to Burning (LFF 2018) finds four strangers’ lives entwined by hidden desires and repressed emotions.

The Last Day

Acclaimed visual artist Rachel Rose gives Mrs Dalloway a contemporary makeover in her arresting mood piece, starring Alicia Vikander and Victoria Pedretti.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "她们是七个女人。身穿长黑裙与白色衬裙。她们充满活力、斗志昂扬、守望相助，却也脆弱。她们在狂喜、痛苦、疯狂、爱意，以及抵抗和希望之间挣扎。《Land of Hope》由瑞士 Compagnie Linga 的卡塔日娜·格达涅茨（Katarzyna Gdaniec）和马尔科·坎塔卢波（Marco Cantalupo）——这对艺术与生活伴侣——创作，取材于这位伟大的米兰女诗人、格言家兼作家阿尔达·梅里尼（Alda Merini）的生平与文本，将其转化为一部礼赞女性力量的创作。灵感源于对她作品的文献研究工作，“我们将工作重心集中在编排上，”两位编舞家表示，“聚焦于她那些尖锐而清醒的格言，它们交织着讽刺、令人不安却又充满诗意的真相。”", "links": [{"text": "Land of hope", "url": "https://www.teatronuovonapoli.it/stagione/land-of-hope/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Land of Hope》（在那不勒斯新剧院为 Körper 艺术季进行意大利首演）以两个女人并肩背立、在半明半暗中移动开场，其中一人的头部反复靠在另一人膝上的动作——随后被其他女舞者重复——标志着该编舞的序幕。她们全部四处游走，仿佛迷失且孤立，在环绕自身的虚空中感到错愕，但又随即通过认出彼此而重新凝聚、汇聚。", "links": [{"text": "Napoli", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/tag/napoli/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "将她们连结在一起的是一种带有间歇的连续节奏，以及一种充满张力的重复动作，这些动作在菲利普·福什（Philippe Foch）的打击乐、马蒂亚斯·德尔普兰克（Mathias Delplanque）混音的电子乐衬托下展开；这些音效勾勒出一个敲击不断的音景，再加上灯光设计日耳曼·施瓦布（German Schwab）营造的氛围所勾勒出的视觉音景。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们在两位编舞家格达涅茨和坎塔卢波那种动态而循环的风格特征中重温了这一点，这种风格伴随着强度的变化，赋予了女舞者们的动作以生命力，她们的肢体痕迹充满整个舞台，使其因能量而震颤。这种能量有时让人联想起带有哀悼色彩的民间舞蹈、民俗而大众的舞蹈（按最深刻的意义理解）、游行与仪式，以及带有原型色彩的地中海风情，其中包含充满仪式感的合唱动作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是一个同心与发散动作的交织与解体、欢乐循环、狂怒爆发的过程，是个体身体的爆发，它们被释放又随即被集团重新吸收，形成人类链条、线条与对角线、穿梭与位移。接着是缠绕与解开，她们拿着用系有小铃铛的线，将其缠绕在双手和手臂上，随后向前推进至前台、摆动骨盆、调整呼吸节奏、打破队列。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在紧凑、迅速、催促的节奏之后，随之而来的是片刻的放松：手臂的下垂、呼吸的平息、视线的悬置、时间的放缓、在地上的拖行。这种松弛并非屈服，而是蓄力，以便继续保持韧性：褪去黑色夹克，只留下宽大的白裙，在旋转中舞动，令人联想到旋转德尔维施（dervishes）。而尾声则具有一种全新默契的动态、重获的冲动，以及另一种喜悦的曙光。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该演出在那不勒斯新剧院（Teatro Nuovo）为 Körper 舞蹈制作国家中心（Körper | Centro Nazionale di Produzione della Danza）的艺术季首演，巡演随后继续：11月5日至7日在日内瓦艺术中心（Centre des Arts Ecolint，瑞士）；10日和11日在奥尔滕舞蹈节（Festival Tanz，瑞士）；并于2027年1月29日和30日重返意大利热那亚的托斯剧院（Teatro della Tosse），格达涅茨和坎塔卢波与该剧院订立了艺术伙伴关系，这一合作关系将这对编舞组合稳固地纳入了节目编排团队中。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Sono sette donne. Vestite con lunghe gonne nere e sottoveste bianca. Sono energiche, agguerrite, solidali. Ma anche fragili. Si dibattono tra esaltazione, dolore, follia, amore. E resistenza, speranza. Land of hope della svizzera Compagnie Linga di Katarzyna Gdaniec e Marco Cantalupo – coppia d’arte e di vita -, attinge al vissuto e ai testi della grande poetessa, aforista e scrittrice milanese Alda Merini , per farne una creazione che celebra la forza femminile. L’ispirazione è nata da un lavoro di documentazione sulla sua opera «Concentrando il lavoro – dichiarano i due coreografi – sui suoi aforismi così taglienti e lucidi, venati di sarcasmo, di verità scomode e al contempo poetiche».

L’inizio di Land of hope (prima nazionale al Teatro Nuovo di Napoli per la rassegna di Körper) con due donne accostate di spalle che si muovono nella penombra e col gesto ripetuto della testa dell’una poggiata sul grembo dell’altra – movimento poi ripreso dalle altre donne -, segna l’incipit della coreografia. Vagando tutte, come se sperse e isolate, sorprese nel vuoto che le circonda, ritrovano subito una compattezza, un convergere riconoscendosi.

Li unisce un ritmo continuo, con pause, e un movimento ripetitivo carico di tensione, sviluppato sulla musica percussiva di Philippe Foch, mixata dall’elettronica di Mathias Delplanque , effetti che scandiscono un paesaggio sonoro martellante al quale si aggiunge quello visivo disegnato dalle atmosfere del light designer German Schwab .

Ritroviamo la cifra stilistica dei due coreografi Gdaniec e Cantalupo in quel flusso dinamico e circolare, con variazioni di intensità, che anima il movimento delle danzatrici le cui tracce gestuali riempiono la scena facendola vibrare di energia. Un’energia che, a tratti, sembra richiamare le danze popolari di un Sud luttuoso, folclorico – popolare, nell’accezione più colta -, di processioni e cerimonie, di un Mediterraneo archetipico, con azioni corali che sanno di ritualità.

È un farsi e disfarsi di movimenti concentrici e divergenti, di gioiose circolarità, di scatti furiosi, di corpi individuali che detonano, lasciati andare e subito riassorbiti nel gruppo a formare catene umane, linee e diagonali, attraversamenti e dislocazioni. E poi viluppi e scioglimenti prendendo dei fili con dei campanelli legati, attorcigliandoli sulle mani e le braccia, quindi avanzare in proscenio, oscillare il bacino, ritmare il respiro, rompere le righe.

Al ritmo serrato, veloce, incalzante, seguono attimi di distensione in quel cedere di braccia, quel quietare il fiato, sospendere gli sguardi, frenare il tempo, trascinarsi a terra: un allentamento che non è resa ma accensione per continuare la resilienza svestendosi delle giacche nere e rimanendo con le ampie gonne bianche mosse in danze circolari che rimandano ai dervisci rotanti. E il finale ha la dinamica di una nuova complicità, un ritrovato slancio, e la luce dell’alba di un’altra gioia.

Lo spettacolo ha debuttato a Napoli al Teatro Nuovo per la rassegna di Körper | Centro Nazionale di Produzione della Danza, e prosegue la tournée al Centre des Arts Ecolint di Ginevra (CH), dal 5 al 7 novembre; al Festival Tanz di Olten (CH), il 10 e 11; e torna in Italia, il 29 e 30 gennaio 2027, a Genova, al Teatro della Tosse, teatro col quale Gdaniec e Cantalupo, hanno stipulato un partenariato artistico, sodalizio che coinvolge stabilmente la coppia di coreografi nel team di programmazione.

Pools, palm trees and pulling a caravan: Australian retro holidays – in pictures

Take a nostalgic look back at how Australians used to holiday throughout the 1950s, 60s and 70s. A new book by Ian Collis features vintage caravans, seaside motels and charming snapshots of summer road trips past

Longboards on the beach in the 1960s. Photograph: New Holland Publishers

Fri 16 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 18.57 EDT

In 1964 John Landi wanted something to make passing traffic stop at his roadside banana stall in Coffs Harbour. He knew it would have to be big, so with local engineer Alan Chapman they designed the Big Banana, now a major tourist attractionPhotograph: Benny Agius

Travellers looking out at a British Overseas Airways Corporation (BOAC) plane on the tarmac at Darwin airport in 1960Photograph: Library & Archives Northern Territory

Bathers enjoying the in-ground swimming pool at the Beachcomber private hotel in Surfers Paradise, in the 1960sPhotograph: National Archives of Australia

El Caballo Blanco, an amusement park on the Hume Highway, 60km from Sydney, was popular during the school holidays with their famous Andalusian horsesPhotograph: New Holland Publishers

Cabins on South Molle Island, one of the Whitsundays’ 74 islands off the central coast of Queensland, in 1963Photograph: National Archives of Australia

editorial_excerpt_zh: 多伦多电影节：这位两届奥斯卡得主饰演一名不寻常的杀手，影片将通俗动作与家庭剧扣人心弦地融为一体。拉蒂夫（Latif）由马赫沙拉·阿里深情演绎，是个神情肃穆的杀手，他的杀人工具包里装着尿布。我说不准这是因为尿布能随手用来吸干成滩的血迹，还是因为这名杀手随时都得从残暴的行当切换到父亲职责。又或许，对这个手持利刃和婴儿湿巾的合同杀手来说，两者皆是：他既夺人性命，也养育生命；他的人生由刺耳而富有诗意的矛盾构成，就像他身处的这部电影。

L atif, the solemn hitman played soulfully by Mahershala Ali , carries diapers in his kill kit. I can’t tell if that’s because they come in handy when soaking up pools of blood on the fly; or because at a moment’s notice the hitman has to switch over from his brutal occupation to daddy duties. Or perhaps it’s both for this contract killer who comes armed with a blade and baby wipes, who takes lives and nurtures them, whose life is composed of jarring and poetic contradictions, much like the movie he’s in.

Those contradictions are on full striking display in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’s opening moments, an explosive close-quarters brawl in a restroom, after which Latif uses the baby wipes to clean up the mess he made with that blade. It’s a lovely image, in a film filled with so many, cutting right through the tension within this character. It also feels like a wink to the audience from Ali and writer/director Bassam Tariq, a way for them to acknowledge right off the top the distracting mess made by that other Blade.

Tariq and Ali were collaborating on Marvel’s Blade reboot . Ali was announced to star as the vampire-slayer formerly played by Wesley Snipes all the way back in 2019. Tariq signed on to write and direct in 2021 but departed a year later. Ali recently revealed that, after being strung along for seven years in development, the reboot was not happening. It’s easy to assume that some of the ideas Tariq and Ali had for Blade made their way into this new collaboration, in which Ali gets to finally wield a blade and John Cho, of Harold and Kumar fame, stuns as a vampiric foe. The echoes and parallels are there but minimal, perhaps even coincidental.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is its own beautiful singular thing, partly a stylish and pulpy neo-western thriller about a father racked with guilt, navigating violence that comes heavy and uneasy, but first and foremost a drama about a family reconciling their Muslim faith with their actions, their environments and their grief.

Both Tariq and Ali are Muslims. The former’s debut, Mogul Mowgli, and his directing work on the Prime Video series Bait, both starring Riz Ahmed, were about young British-Pakistani men who internalize hostility towards their faith. In Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, Tariq builds an even more nuanced portrait of faith around Ali, who seizes the rare opportunity to explore his religion onscreen.

Ali’s Latif, who once taught kids at prayer school, fashions himself as a righteous killer with a code, meting out justice to those who offend Islam. Getting paid for it is beside the point, he argues, when a supportive but critical Imam played by Giancarlo Esposito takes Latif to task.

As the film opens, when Latif is bashing that victim’s head against a bathroom sink and unceremoniously tying up his corpse, his own wife (Shakirah DeMesier) lies there dying, her body delicately cared for by their community in Houston (the movie was shot in Atlanta). That leaves Latif a widower who, alongside his eldest, Fatiha (Adia, quietly mesmerizing), cares for a curious young son (Jahleel Kamara) and infant daughter who won’t take formula.

So much of Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is propelled by Latif’s frantic search for breast milk, inspired by the writer and director’s own ordeal when his wife fell ill. Ali is especially breathtaking in these moments, with Latif looking weathered and exasperated, but fighting to maintain his wits and composure, as he’s turned away from a milk bank that requires a prescription and accosted by a doctor in the family (Tramell Tillman) when seeking help. Latif finally has to square the assistance he gets from a breastfeeding sex worker (Tiffany Boone) with his at times rigid and hypocritical moral and religious code.

Those negotiations are constant and granular. At every turn, Latif and Fatiha figure out how to make their Islamic faith work for who they are and the situations they’re in. How important is fasting when your frantic ordeals make you forget to eat altogether? How do we grapple with scriptures that limit growth and empathy, but not ignore the profound lessons also found in those texts? In the grand scheme of things, does it matter that your adolescent daughter is using the Mormon neighbour’s wifi to watch Furry porn, which must be all kinds of Haram? These are the questions that make Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother so grounded, compassionate, and, dare I say, divine.

That spiritual journey is also the bridge between the intimate family story and the thriller plot. Latif finds himself caught in a beef between his employer’s son, a producer of “Habibi porn” (Abubakr Ali) who tests what the former stands for, and Cho’s Pastor Hwan Yoon. The latter, captivating in a gold grill, cowboy hat and southern drawl, is an Iraq war veteran who turned evangelical after he supposedly rose back from the dead on the battlefield. His heel turn towards religious fanaticism means surrounding himself with tooled-up mercenaries and preaching about Christ at gunpoint.

Tariq deftly navigates the divide between Latif and Pastor Hwan, setting up binaries and conflicts that could easily give in to Muslim versus Christian sensationalism. But his approach is soulful and considered, allowing everyone their convictions and bandwidth for the mercy and grace the movie ultimately preaches about.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother isn’t just interrogating faith. It’s embracing and appreciating those jarring and poetic contradictions that come with the territory.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is premiering at the Toronto film festival and opens in select theaters in New York City and Los Angeles on 25 September, following a wider release on 2 October and 9 October. It is released in the UK on 20 November

article_text:
Lin-Manuel Miranda has announced the cast for his next Broadway venture, “ Warriors ,” which comes a decade after “Hamilton” became a pop culture sensation.

The upcoming production, which opens in the spring, will star Jaci Calderon, Aneesa Folds, Amber Gray, Julia Harriman, Sasha Hutchings, Gizel Jiménez, Jasmine Cephas Jones, Kenita R. Miller, Sasha Allen, Casey Likes, and Donald Webber Jr. — several of whom have either worked on prior iterations of “Warriors” or appeared in Miranda’s other shows, “Hamilton” and “In the Heights. Additional cast members will be announced at a later date.

Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart

“Warriors” will begin previews at the Lunt-Fontanne Theatre on March 9 ahead of opening night on April 8.

“Warriors” features a book, music and lyrics by co-writers Miranda and Eisa Davis. Based on Sol Yurick’s 1965 novel and Paramount’s 1979 action film, “Warriors” follows a fictional New York gang from the Bronx to their home turf in Coney Island after they’re framed for the murder of a respected gang leader. The movie version of “Warriors” isn’t a musical, but it does feature songs by Barry De Vorzon, Joe Walsh and Arnold McCuller. The stage show originated as a 2024 concept album, executive produced by Nas and produced by musician Mike Elizondo. It featured the voices of Ms. Lauryn Hill, Busta Rhymes, Marc Anthony, Billy Porter, Ghostface Killah, RZA, Colman Domingo, Cam’ron, and Kim Dracula.

“We’re having the time of our lives making ‘Warriors.’ It’s a rollercoaster like the Coney Island Cyclone, with all the action of Walter Hill’s classic film,” Miranda and Davis said in a statement. “It’s a New York story to the bone, with music steeped in all the genres that were born and revolutionized here, from hip-hop to salsa to ska and metal and everything in between. It’s an edge-of-your-seat journey from Brooklyn to the Bronx and back again. It’s a dream of a more peaceful city where we all come home alive. This is the sound of something being born.”

“Warriors” will be directed by Jenny Koons and co-directed and choreographed by Andy Blankenbuehler, a Tony winner who worked with Miranda on “In the Heights” and “Hamilton.” Producers include Thomas Kail (“Hamilton”), Miranda and his father, Luis A. Miranda, Jr., and Jeffrey Seller. “Warriors” features scenic design by David Korins, costume design by Dede Ayite, lighting design by Natasha Katz, sound design by Jason Crystal, projection design by Hana S. Kim, fight direction by Drew Leary, music supervision by Kurt Crowley, and orchestrations by Kurt Crowley, Mike Elizondo and Scott Wasserman.

Toen mijn ouders ontdekten dat ik het misschien iets té leuk vond en ik zei dat ik naar de kunstacademie wilde, zeiden ze: “Nee, laat het maar een hobby blijven.” Ze konden zich een leven als kunstenaar niet voorstellen. Daarom ging ik naar een technische universiteit, eerst in China, daarna in Duitsland en Nederland. Pas tijdens mijn promotie in cognitieve psychologie begon ik aan de Gerrit Rietveld Academie te studeren. Doordat ik de parttime-opleiding Dogtime volgde, kon ik mijn kunstopleiding afronden naast mijn onderzoekswerk. Kort na mijn afstuderen besloot ik fulltime kunstenaar te worden. Het voelde alsof ik terugkeerde naar iets wat ik altijd al had willen doen.

Je zei dat je een lifelong bird keeper bent. Bedoel je dat letterlijk?

Ja. Ik had al huisvogels voordat ik naar school ging. Mijn vader kocht mijn eerste paar grasparkieten. Daarna bleef ik vogels houden. Toen ik op de kleuterschool zat, had ik ook duiven als huisdieren. Dat was toen heel populair in Noord-China, vooral postduiven die hun weg terug konden vinden. Ik had op een gegeven moment vijftien tot twintig duiven op mijn balkon. Als ik er nu op terugkijk, denk ik dat ik ze misschien niet had moeten houden, want het was erg rommelig en het waren niet de juiste omstandigheden voor ze. Maar ze zijn wel een belangrijk onderdeel van mijn jeugdherinneringen geworden. Op dit moment heb ik twee Bourkes parkieten en een valkparkiet. In mijn schilderijen zie je soms roze vogels. Die komen niet uit mijn verbeelding, zo zien mijn vogels er daadwerkelijk uit.

Wat symboliseren vogels in je werk?

Voor mij zijn het in de eerste plaats gewoon vogels. Het zijn echte wezens die met mij samenleven. Ik schilder ze alsof ze mijn huisgenoten zijn, gewoon aanwezig in de ruimte. Maar toch, als je vraagt of ze symbolisch zijn, zou ik zeggen: een beetje. Ik ben me ervan bewust dat het een bijzonder gezicht is. In een gewone, huiselijke omgeving een vogel vrij zien rondvliegen, dat is op zichzelf al iets magisch. Voor mij kunnen ze een symbool zijn voor een leven elders. Veel mensen leiden een alledaags leven, maar vragen zich af: wat als het leven iets anders zou kunnen zijn. Dat gevoel heb ik zelf lange tijd gehad. Toen ik nog bij een bedrijf werkte, stelde ik me voor: wat als ik schilder zou kunnen zijn? Dat idee bleef me lange tijd achtervolgen. Soms kan ik naar mijn vogels kijken en even mentaal ontsnappen aan de werkelijkheid. Je ziet dat idee ook terug in de kleine ramen in mijn schilderijen. In één schilderij zie je bijvoorbeeld vanuit een koelkast de lucht en de sterren.

Bedoel je het schilderij Chores, met wel twintig duiven op het aanrecht?

Ja, en vooral die koelkast is voor mij een sterk symbool: je bent bezig met dat soort dagelijkse dingen en wilt daar even aan ontsnappen, om ergens anders naartoe te kunnen dwalen.

De vogels wijzen je de weg. Hoe reageerden je ouders toen je fulltime kunstenaar werd?

Voor mijn afstuderen hadden we daar moeilijke gesprekken over. Vooral mijn moeder was er aanvankelijk sterk op tegen. Maar ik weet dat ze het goed bedoelde. In de Chinese cultuur is een vaste baan heel belangrijk. Na mijn afstuderen zag mijn moeder hoeveel doorzettingsvermogen ik had en dat ik ook erkenning kreeg. Uiteindelijk dacht ze: als dit het enige is wat je gelukkig maakt, ga dan maar door. Er is iets wat me bijzonder heeft geraakt. Nadat ik mijn baan had opgezegd, zei mijn moeder dat ze me iets cadeau wilde geven. Ze vond dat ik een echt Chinese manier van signeren moest hebben en liet daarom een kunstenaar een stenen stempel voor me maken, zoals je die ziet bij Chinese schilderkunst en kalligrafie.

Dat is zo mooi.

Ja, dat raakte me echt. Ik moest ervan huilen. Na dertig jaar… dat was een heel bijzonder moment voor me.

Als ik het goed begrijp, ben je opgegroeid met vogels en andere dieren om je heen. Je ziet ze als je broers en zussen, als vrienden, of gewoon als wezens. En ze bieden je een manier om na te denken over verschillende mogelijkheden van perceptie en van leven. Ik vraag me af: zijn er andere kunstenaars die je verbeelding voeden?

Er zijn veel kunstenaars die ik goed vind, mensen zoals Anthony Cudahy, Aubrey Levinthal en Peter Doig. Recentelijk ben ik ook erg aangetrokken tot de portretschilderijen van Elizabeth Peyton, vooral vanwege haar losse penseelstreken. Ik ben figuratief schilder en begin altijd vanuit mijn persoonlijke fotoarchief. Mijn schilderijen gaan vaak over heel intieme situaties, in plaats van over grote, spectaculaire thema’s. Daarom let ik op kunstenaars die vergelijkbare onderwerpen schilderen en die iets bijzonders weten te maken van het alledaagse. Deze kunstenaars werken ook vanuit foto’s, uit hun persoonlijke archief of vanuit gevonden afbeeldingen. Maar hun schilderijen zijn nooit simpelweg reproducties. Je kunt zien waar het schilderen begint. Je ziet de keuzes die ze maken, hoe ze iets opener of ambiguer maken en je ziet hun penseelstreken. Dat fascineert me. Daar ben ik zelf ook voortdurend mee bezig: hoe begin je met een fotografische referentie, maar ga je daar vervolgens voorbij? Hoe bereik je een geschilderde kwaliteit en maak je een schilderij dat interessant blijft om naar te kijken? Ik speel daarbij veel met kleur. Ik gebruik vaak een fluorescerend kleurenpalet, vooral neonroze. Ik begon die kleur te gebruiken tijdens mijn studie aan de Gerrit Rietveld Academie, toen ik onderzoek deed naar het gezichtsvermogen van vogels. Vogels zien een veel breder kleurenspectrum dan mensen, ze kunnen bijvoorbeeld ultraviolet licht zien. Ik ben gaan experimenteren met de vraag hoe je kleuren die wij niet kunnen waarnemen toch in een schilderij kunt representeren.

Daardoor creëer je ook dat dromerige, alsof het beelden zijn die zich zowel op aarde als in een alternatieve, meer absurde realiteit afspelen. Hoe kies je de foto’s uit die je gaat schilderen?

Wanneer ik met een foto werk, probeer ik eerst te begrijpen wat me ertoe bracht om die foto te maken. Daarna vraag ik me af waarom ik juist deze foto uit mijn archief heb gekozen om er een schilderij van te maken. Ik wil het gevoel dat me in eerste instantie aantrok kunnen vangen.

Kun je daar een voorbeeld van geven?

Dodo is een schilderij van een vogel die op de buik van mijn man ligt, terwijl hij gewoon op de bank ligt te rusten. Wat me raakt, is dat het een tafereel is dat ik zelf vaak zie, maar veel mensen kunnen zich misschien moeilijk voorstellen dat een vogel zich zo comfortabel op iemands lichaam voelt. Ik vind die aanraking tussen huid en veren heel mooi. Dat een vogel zo dichtbij kan zijn en mensen zo kan vertrouwen. Die vogel is helaas een paar jaar geleden overleden.

O nee.

Toen ik het schilderij maakte, wilde ik niet dat het fotorealistisch zou worden. Misschien is dat ook waarom ik de vogel alleen als contour heb geschilderd, bijna transparant. Het is een wezen dat er niet meer is. De buik trekt me aan. Ik vind die interessant en ook grappig om te zien. De rest van het lichaam is voor mij minder belangrijk. In het schilderij blijft alleen een fragment over: een vogel op een buik.

Heel mooi. Ik ben ook benieuwd naar het schilderij Bystander . Ik kan het niet helemaal plaatsen. Ik zie een duif en zijn dat gieren?

Ja, dat klopt. Het zijn gieren. Ik zag dat tafereel in Artis in Amsterdam. De dierentuin vind ik fascinerend omdat je er dieren ziet die je anders nooit zou tegenkomen. Het is bijna een monument voor dieren. Je ziet er ook ontmoetingen tussen verschillende soorten die in de natuur bijna onmogelijk zouden zijn. Ze hebben bijvoorbeeld een grote ruimte voor gieren. De tralies zijn breed genoeg voor kleine vogels om naar binnen te vliegen, maar de gieren kunnen er niet uit. Er zitten daardoor voortdurend duiven en andere kleine vogels, zoals eksters en mussen, in de ruimte van de gieren. Dat is een bizarre situatie. De gieren zijn natuurlijk gevaarlijke vogels en de medewerkers voeren ze rauw vlees. Op het schilderij zie je twee gieren die van een lamsbeen eten, terwijl er vlak naast hen een duif staat te kijken. Duiven zijn nogal dom en nieuwsgierig, dus die staat daar gewoon heel dicht bij en kijkt wat er gebeurt.

Je lijkt hem inderdaad niet als een symbool van onschuld tegenover het monsterlijke neer te zetten. Hij lijkt gewoon te denken: what’s up ?

In het schilderij heb ik het wel iets dramatischer gemaakt. Het is alsof ze midden op een podium staan. Er valt een soort spotlight op de achterkant van de gieren. Het is een beetje een verontrustende scène, omdat de gieren het bloederige dode vlees eten. En ondertussen staat die duif daar zo onschuldig naar te kijken. Hij bevindt zich in een compleet andere wereld.

Over de Buning Brongers Prijzen De Buning Brongers Prijs is een Nederlandse kunstprijs voor jonge beeldend kunstenaars. De prijzen worden eens in de twee jaar uitgereikt door de Buning Brongers Stichting uit de nalatenschap van Johan Buning en zijn familie. De prijs bestaat dit jaar 60 jaar en is sinds 1966 uitgereikt aan 174 kunstenaars. Aan de prijs is een geldbedrag verbonden van € 4.500 per winnaar. De kandidaten voor de prijs zijn de afgelopen twee jaar afgestudeerd aan kunstacademies in Nederland en voorgedragen door hun academie. De prijsuitreiking en opening van de tentoonstelling van de zes winnaars vinden plaats op vrijdag 13 november in Arti et Amicitiae te Amsterdam. Je bent van harte uitgenodigd hierbij aanwezig te zijn.

Een gesprek over kunst en kwaliteit in Spui 25 Voorafgaand aan de prijsuitreiking in Arti et Amicitiae organiseert de stichting een gesprek over kunst en kwaliteit in Spui 25. Hans den Hartog Jager en Heske ten Cate geven elk een presentatie waarin ze dieper ingaan op hun persoonlijke ervaringen en inzichten. Aansluitend gaan Dineke Blom, Ricardo van Eyk en Robert Zandvliet met elkaar in gesprek. Je bent ook hier van harte welkom!

article_text:
Di Venezia conosciamo bene l’immagine: sappiamo riconoscerne gli edifici storici, i profili dei tetti, i canali punteggiati dalle gondole cariche di turisti e persino certe strette insenature tra gli edifici. Molto meno familiare è, invece, tutto ciò che permette a questa immagine anfibia di continuare a esistere: il lavoro di chi ripara un lampione, le abitudini degli animali che ne attraversano gli spazi e gli usi spontanei che trasformano un luogo pubblico in un rifugio temporaneo.

È su questa distanza tra la città che si mostra e quella che quotidianamente la produce che interviene Typing Bird , progetto di Pietro Vedovato e Federico Zeltman , presentato negli spazi di Panorama fino al prossimo 15 novembre. Attraverso quattro racconti affidati allo sguardo anomalo di un gabbiano, l’esposizione sposta infatti l’attenzione dalle architetture ai comportamenti, dai luoghi alle relazioni che li attraversano, restituendo così una Venezia certo meno monumentale, ma più intima e inaspettata.

D’altronde è proprio questo la vocazione di Panorama, fin dalla sua apertura nel 2023 : con i suoi circa venti metri quadrati, la pianta triangolare e le grandi vetrine affacciate sul campiello, lo spazio porta avanti progetti che riescono a rappresentare il concetto stesso di insularità sotto nuove prospettive. Come il gabbiano di Vedovato e Zeltman, anche Panorama si sottrae alla pretesa di offrire una visione complessiva, ma ci restituisce piuttosto episodi circoscritti, incontri e dettagli che acquistano significato proprio perché messi in relazione.

Ma, per comprendere meglio quest’attitudine, entriamo nel vivo di Typing Bird , che prende la forma di un ufficio spoglio, con una scrivania di cartone, un monito acceso e un gabbiano impagliato a fare da guardiano e narratore. Gli oggetti che compongono l’ambiente sono quelli familiari di una postazione di lavoro, eppure la loro funzione appare sospesa. L’ufficio diventa così un ambiente temporaneamente sottratto al proprio impiego originario, e gli elementi presenti vengono riutilizzati e ricombinati secondo una logica inaspettata: una piccola appropriazione che richiama quei processi attraverso cui gli abitanti, umani e non umani, trasformano continuamente gli spazi urbani.

Sul monitor, davanti al quale il gabbiano sembra essersi insediato, scorrono i quattro racconti che compongono il progetto: storie che seguono il lavoro di un elettricista incaricato della manutenzione dei lampioni veneziani; di un gatto che attraversa i padiglioni della Biennale; di due ragazzi che trovano riparo dalla pioggia sotto una rovina architettonica. L’ultimo episodio mette invece in relazione un netsuke giapponese a forma di coniglio, custodito al Museo d’Arte Orientale di Ca’ Pesaro, con un coniglio di plastica esposto nella vetrina di un negozio: duo oggetti apparentemente lontanissimi, accomunati dallo sguardo di un guardiano.

A cambiare, in ciascuna storia, è soprattutto il modo in cui vengono osservati luoghi e oggetti che crediamo di conoscere. Come spiegano gli artisti, «studiare e monitorare il quotidiano, cercando di mettere in luce nuovi percorsi generati involontariamente dal comportamento di chi vive in città, ci è parso più utile che concentrarci unicamente sullo spazio urbano». Da qui la scelta di considerare gli abitanti, umani e non umani, come «potenziali collaboratori».

È interessante, allora, tornare alla scrivania che accoglie il visitatore all’ingresso della mostra. L’ufficio, privato della propria funzione ordinaria, diventa il luogo di un’appropriazione imprevista: il gabbiano occupa la postazione di lavoro, si impossessa degli strumenti e li utilizza per raccontare una città che gli esseri umani hanno costruito, ma che non appartiene esclusivamente a loro. In questa piccola inversione di ruoli si ritrova anche qualcosa della naturai Panorama: uno spazio nato dalla trasformazione di un ex locale commerciale, sottratto alla propria destinazione originaria e restituito alla città come luogo di incontro e produzione culturale: due operazioni diverse, ma attraversate dalla stessa possibilità di immaginare usi ulteriori per ciò che già esiste.
